relationship: related written preservation of a vision
rationale: Daniel writes the vision in principal points; Habakkuk is commanded to write a vision clearly on a boxwood tablet. The connection concerns recording the revelation, without equating the visions or their writing materials.
source_text: In the first year of Baltasar’s reign over the country of Babylonia, Daniel saw a vision at his head upon his bed. Then Daniel wrote the vision he had seen in principal points:

target_units.text: The Lord answered me: “Write a vision clearly on a boxwood tablet, so that the one reading these things may pursue them.

relationship: related visionary use of the four winds of heaven
rationale: Daniel sees heaven's four winds falling upon the sea. In Zechariah the four chariots are explained as heaven's four winds going to stand beside the Lord. The shared expression belongs to different visionary scenes, not identical vehicles or actions.
source_text: “Upon my bed I was watching in dreams by night, and there were four winds of heaven falling upon the great sea.

target_units.text: I answered and said to the angel speaking within me, “What are these, lord?”
The angel speaking within me answered, “These are the four winds of heaven; they go out to stand beside the Lord of all the earth.

relationship: same-chapter interpretation of the four beasts
rationale: The four differing beasts rising from the sea are expressly interpreted as four kingdoms that will perish from the earth. The native interpretation says perish, not merely arise.
source_text: Four beasts came up from the sea, each differing from the other.

target_units.text: ‘These great beasts are four kingdoms that will perish from the earth.

relationship: contrasting transformations with lion, eagle and changed-heart imagery
rationale: The lioness has eagle-like wings and receives a human heart. Nebuchadnezzar describes eagle-like hair, lion-like nails and changed flesh and heart while living with animals before his restoration. These distinctive images support a literary comparison without identifying the lioness as that king.
source_text: The first was like a lioness with wings like an eagle’s. I watched until her wings were plucked out, she was lifted from the earth and stood on human feet, and a human heart was given her.

target_units.text: “I, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, was bound for seven years. They fed me grass like an ox, and I ate the earth’s greenery. After seven years I devoted my soul to supplication and pleaded concerning my sins before the Lord, the God of heaven; concerning my acts of ignorance I entreated the great God of gods.

My hair became like an eagle’s wings, and my nails like a lion’s. My flesh and my heart were changed; I walked naked with the wild animals of the earth. I saw a dream, and apprehensions seized me. After a time a deep sleep took hold of me, and drowsiness fell upon me.

At the completion of the seven years, the time of my release came. My sins and my acts of ignorance reached their full measure before the God of heaven. I entreated the great God of gods concerning my acts of ignorance, and an angel called to me from heaven, saying, ‘Nebuchadnezzar, serve the holy God of heaven and give glory to the Most High; the kingship of your nation is restored to you.’

relationship: close fourth-kingdom imagery of iron and overpowering destruction
rationale: The fourth beast has iron teeth and crushes and tramples; the earlier interpretation calls the fourth kingdom strong like iron that subdues everything. The texts share the fourth position and iron imagery without supplying a later historical name.
source_text: After this I watched in the night vision a fourth beast, fearsome, its terror surpassing in strength. It had great iron teeth, devoured and pounded, trampled all around with its feet, and acted differently from all the beasts before it. It had ten horns,

target_units.text: A fourth kingdom will be strong like iron that subdues everything and cuts down every tree, and the whole earth will be shaken.

relationship: same-chapter interpretation of the emerging horn's hostility
rationale: The new horn causes three earlier horns to wither, speaks great things and wars against the holy ones. The explanation describes another king humbling three kings, speaking against the Most High and wearing down His holy ones.
source_text: and many plans were in its horns. Another single horn sprouted among them, small among its horns, and three of the earlier horns were withered through it. This horn had eyes like human eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and it made war against the holy ones.

target_units.text: As for the kingdom’s ten horns, ten kings will arise, and another king will arise after them. He will surpass the earlier ones in evils and humble three kings.
He will speak words against the Most High, wear down the holy ones of the Most High, and expect to alter seasons and law. Everything will be handed into his hands for a time, times, and half a time.

relationship: parallel throne visions with human-form and fire imagery
rationale: Daniel sees the Ancient of Days seated on a throne like a flame; Ezekiel sees a human-like form above a throne and fire-like brightness around the appearance of the Lord's glory. Snow-white clothing and hair belong specifically to Daniel's description.
source_text: I watched until thrones were set in place and an Ancient of Days was seated, wearing a covering like snow, with the hair of His head like pure white wool. The throne was like a flame of fire,

target_units.text: Like the appearance of a sapphire stone was the likeness of a throne upon it; and above the likeness of the throne was a likeness like the form of a human being.

I saw something like the sight of electrum from the appearance of a waist upward; and from the appearance of a waist down below I saw something like the appearance of fire, with its brightness all around.

Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

relationship: parallel heavenly throne scenes with attending multitudes and deliberation
rationale: Daniel's multitude of attendants stand beside the enthroned figure as a court sits. Micaiah sees the heavenly army around the Lord's throne and hears deliberation concerning Ahab. Daniel additionally describes a fiery river and opened books.
source_text: and a river of fire came out before Him. A thousand thousands attended Him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood beside Him. A court sat, and books were opened.

target_units.text: Micaiah said, “Not so—not I! Hear the Lord’s word—not so! I saw the Lord, the God of Israel, sitting on His throne, and all the army of heaven stood around Him, on His right and His left.
The Lord said, ‘Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Remmath-gilead?’ One said this, and another said that.
A spirit came forward, stood before the Lord, and said, ‘I will deceive him.’ The Lord said to it, ‘By what means?’
It said, ‘I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ He said, ‘You will deceive him and indeed prevail. Go out and do so.’

relationship: same-chapter correspondence between the beast's destruction and judgment on authority
rationale: The beast whose horn speaks great words is killed and given to fire. The later explanation places the destruction of authority at the sitting of judgment; it does not repeat the burning-body detail.
source_text: Then I watched the sound of the great words the horn was speaking. The beast was beaten to death, its body perished, and it was given over to burning fire.

target_units.text: The judgment will sit; they will destroy the authority and plan to defile and destroy completely.

relationship: related removal of royal authority within appointed times
rationale: Authority is removed while a span of life remains for a time and season. Daniel's earlier praise says God changes seasons and times and transfers and appoints kings. The limited extension of life is peculiar to the later vision.
source_text: He removed those around it from their authority, and a span of life was given them for a time and a season.

target_units.text: He changes seasons and times, transfers kings and appoints them, gives wisdom to the wise and understanding to those who possess knowledge,

relationship: close Son-of-Man coming upon heaven's clouds
rationale: Daniel depicts one like a son of man coming upon heaven's clouds; Matthew describes the Son of Man coming upon those clouds. Daniel's supplied text says he was present as an Ancient of Days; it is not paraphrased as approaching a separate Ancient of Days. Matthew places the image in Jesus' account of His coming.
source_text: I watched in the night vision, and there, upon the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man was coming. He was present as an Ancient of Days, and those standing by were present with him.

target_units.text: Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn; they will see the Son of Man coming upon the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.

relationship: Jesus' trial declaration using the Son-of-Man cloud image
rationale: Jesus answers the high priest by speaking of the Son of Man coming with heaven's clouds, corresponding to Daniel's cloud-borne figure. Mark additionally mentions sitting at the right of the Power; Daniel here says present as an Ancient of Days.
source_text: I watched in the night vision, and there, upon the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man was coming. He was present as an Ancient of Days, and those standing by were present with him.

target_units.text: He remained silent and answered nothing. Again the high priest questioned Him and said to Him, “Art Thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?”
Jesus said, “I am. And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”

relationship: close promise of a kingdom never destroyed
rationale: The cloud-borne figure receives everlasting authority and an indestructible kingdom. The earlier interpretation says the God of heaven will establish a kingdom that stands forever and is not destroyed. The kingdom's permanence is shared, while the source explicitly describes authority being given.
source_text: Authority was given him, and all the nations of the earth according to their families, and all glory, worshipped him. His authority is everlasting authority that will never be taken away, and his kingdom will never be destroyed.

target_units.text: In the times of these kings the God of heaven will establish another kingdom, which will exist for ever and will not be destroyed. This kingdom will not leave another nation; it will strike and obliterate these kingdoms and will itself stand for ever,

relationship: related everlasting royal dominion in the promise concerning Jesus
rationale: Daniel's figure receives authority that will never be taken away and a kingdom never destroyed. Gabriel announces Jesus' reign over Jacob's house forever and a kingdom without end. Luke explicitly names Jesus and David's throne; those names are not inserted into Daniel's wording.
source_text: Authority was given him, and all the nations of the earth according to their families, and all glory, worshipped him. His authority is everlasting authority that will never be taken away, and his kingdom will never be destroyed.

target_units.text: And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son, and you shall name Him Jesus.
He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David,
and He will reign over Jacob’s house forever, and His kingdom will have no end.”

relationship: same-chapter framing by the seer's distress
rationale: Daniel's disheartened response during the vision corresponds to his final astonishment and changed condition at the account's end. The two responses frame the intervening request and interpretation.
source_text: I, Daniel, was disheartened by these things in the night vision,

target_units.text: Until the account ended, I, Daniel, was greatly overcome with astonishment; my condition changed, and I fixed the matter in my heart.”

relationship: parallel requests for interpretation of symbolic visions
rationale: Daniel asks one standing there for exact understanding and receives an explanation of the beasts. Zechariah asks the speaking angel about the chariots and receives their interpretation as four winds. The request-and-interpretation pattern does not equate the symbols.
source_text: and approached one of those standing there, seeking exact understanding from him concerning all these things. He answered me and explained the judgment of the words:

target_units.text: I answered and said to the angel speaking within me, “What are these, lord?”
The angel speaking within me answered, “These are the four winds of heaven; they go out to stand beside the Lord of all the earth.

relationship: related sequences of four kingdoms in interpreted visions
rationale: The beasts are explained as four kingdoms destined to perish. The earlier interpretation progresses from Nebuchadnezzar's golden head through later kingdoms to a fourth kingdom. The sequences are compared without assigning unnamed kingdoms historical identities.
source_text: ‘These great beasts are four kingdoms that will perish from the earth.

target_units.text: You, O king, are king of kings, and the Lord of heaven has given you rule, kingdom, strength, honor, and glory.
Throughout the inhabited world He has handed over into your hands human beings, wild beasts, birds of heaven, and fish of the sea, to rule them all. You are the golden head.
After you a kingdom lesser than you will arise, and another, a third kingdom of bronze, which will rule the whole earth.
A fourth kingdom will be strong like iron that subdues everything and cuts down every tree, and the whole earth will be shaken.

relationship: parallel gift of the kingdom to God's people
rationale: The holy ones will receive and hold the kingdom; Jesus tells the little flock that their Father was pleased to give them the kingdom. Daniel expressly adds possession for the age of ages.
source_text: The holy ones of the Most High will receive the kingdom and hold the kingdom for ever, for the age of ages.’

target_units.text: Do not fear, little flock, because your Father was pleased to give you the kingdom.

relationship: same-chapter reprise of the fourth beast's iron teeth and trampling
rationale: Daniel's request repeats the fourth beast's terror, iron teeth, devouring and trampling from the vision. It adds bronze claws, so the later description is not treated as an exact duplicate.
source_text: Then I wanted exact understanding of the fourth beast, which destroyed everything and was exceedingly fearsome. Its teeth were iron and its claws bronze, devouring everyone all around and trampling with its feet,

target_units.text: After this I watched in the night vision a fourth beast, fearsome, its terror surpassing in strength. It had great iron teeth, devoured and pounded, trampled all around with its feet, and acted differently from all the beasts before it. It had ten horns,

relationship: same-chapter interpretation of the ten horns and displaced three
rationale: The ten horns and the later horn through which three fall are explained as ten kings and another king who humbles three. The explanation supplies the royal meaning of the particular horn configuration.
source_text: and of its ten horns upon its head and the single other that sprouted, through which three fell out. That horn had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and its appearance surpassed the others.

target_units.text: As for the kingdom’s ten horns, ten kings will arise, and another king will arise after them. He will surpass the earlier ones in evils and humble three kings.

relationship: related hostile power attacking holy people
rationale: The horn wars against the holy ones and routes them; the later vision describes a ruler who destroys rulers and a people of holy ones. Both depict holy people suffering under hostile power, without declaring the two figures historically identical.
source_text: I observed that horn waging war against the holy ones and routing them,

target_units.text: His strength will be made firm, though not by his own strength. He will destroy astonishingly, prosper, and act; he will destroy rulers and a people of holy ones.

relationship: related participation of the holy ones in judgment
rationale: Daniel says judgment is given to the holy ones, who take possession of kingship. Paul says the saints will judge the world and angels. The target makes their judging activity explicit; Daniel's judgment-given wording is preserved.
source_text: until the Ancient of Days came and gave judgment to the holy ones of the Most High. The time was given, and the holy ones took possession of the kingship.

target_units.text: Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is judged by you, are you unworthy of the smallest cases?
Do you not know that we will judge angels, to say nothing of matters of ordinary life?

relationship: close explanation of an overpowering fourth kingdom
rationale: The fourth beast means a kingdom overturning and grinding down the earth. The earlier fourth kingdom is likened to iron that subdues everything, and the whole earth will be shaken. Both explanations connect the fourth power with comprehensive destructive force.
source_text: I was told concerning the fourth beast that a fourth kingdom would be upon the earth, surpassing the whole earth, overturning it and grinding it down.

target_units.text: A fourth kingdom will be strong like iron that subdues everything and cuts down every tree, and the whole earth will be shaken.

relationship: same-chapter royal explanation linked to the observed horns
rationale: Ten kings and a later king who humbles three interpret the ten horns and the horn through which three fell. The link keeps the observed symbol beside its explicit royal explanation rather than adding names.
source_text: As for the kingdom’s ten horns, ten kings will arise, and another king will arise after them. He will surpass the earlier ones in evils and humble three kings.

target_units.text: and of its ten horns upon its head and the single other that sprouted, through which three fell out. That horn had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and its appearance surpassed the others.

relationship: close time-times-half-a-time language concerning the holy people
rationale: The hostile king receives power for a time, times and half a time. The later oath repeats that duration in connection with completion of the holy people's hands of release. The unusual latter phrase is preserved, without converting either statement into a dated calendar calculation.
source_text: He will speak words against the Most High, wear down the holy ones of the Most High, and expect to alter seasons and law. Everything will be handed into his hands for a time, times, and half a time.

target_units.text: I heard the one clothed in fine linen above the river’s water say, “Until the time of completion.” He raised his right hand and his left to heaven and swore by God who lives for ever that in a time, times, and half a time would be the completion of the “hands of release” of a holy people, and all these things would be completed.

relationship: contrast between attempted alteration and God's authority over times
rationale: The hostile king expects to alter seasons and law; Daniel's earlier praise attributes changing seasons and times to God. The contrast concerns authority over times, while alteration of law is additional in the hostile king's description.
source_text: He will speak words against the Most High, wear down the holy ones of the Most High, and expect to alter seasons and law. Everything will be handed into his hands for a time, times, and half a time.

target_units.text: He changes seasons and times, transfers kings and appoints them, gives wisdom to the wise and understanding to those who possess knowledge,

relationship: related destruction of earthly authority at the advent of enduring rule
rationale: The sitting judgment is followed by destruction of authority. The earlier interpretation announces a kingdom established by God that obliterates the other kingdoms and stands forever. The comparison does not resolve the source's unspecified plural agents.
source_text: The judgment will sit; they will destroy the authority and plan to defile and destroy completely.

target_units.text: In the times of these kings the God of heaven will establish another kingdom, which will exist for ever and will not be destroyed. This kingdom will not leave another nation; it will strike and obliterate these kingdoms and will itself stand for ever,

relationship: parallel assignment of kingdom rule to a faithful people
rationale: Daniel describes kingdom and rule given to a holy people of the Most High. Jesus assigns a kingdom to those who remained with Him in trials and promises them thrones judging Israel's tribes. The groups and stated scope are kept distinct.
source_text: He gave the kingdom, authority, their greatness, and rule over all the kingdoms under heaven to a holy people of the Most High, to reign with everlasting kingship; all authorities will be subject to him and obey him.

target_units.text: And you are those who have remained with Me in My trials.
And I assign to you a kingdom, just as My Father assigned one to Me,
so that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom, and you will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

relationship: related preservation of a dream report in the heart or mind
rationale: Daniel fixes the vision's matter in his heart after astonishment. After Joseph's dream of the heavenly bodies, his father keeps the saying in mind. The shared response is retaining a dream's significance, not an identification of their dreams.
source_text: Until the account ended, I, Daniel, was greatly overcome with astonishment; my condition changed, and I fixed the matter in my heart.”

target_units.text: And he saw another dream, and told it to his father and to his brothers, and said, “Behold, I have dreamed another dream, as though the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”
And his father rebuked him, and said to him, “What is this dream which you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow down to you to the earth?”
And his brothers envied him, but his father kept the saying in mind.

relationship: explicit retrospective connection to the earlier vision under Baltasar
rationale: The third-year vision is introduced as following the first one. The earlier account dates Daniel's recorded vision to Baltasar's first year. The connection preserves the two stated dates and their narrative sequence.
source_text: In the third year of Baltasar’s reign came the vision that I, Daniel, saw after seeing the first one.

target_units.text: In the first year of Baltasar’s reign over the country of Babylonia, Daniel saw a vision at his head upon his bed. Then Daniel wrote the vision he had seen in principal points:

relationship: same-chapter interpretation of the horned ram
rationale: The horned ram is subsequently identified as the king of the Medes and Persians. The differing horn heights are preserved without assigning a separate historical name to each horn.
source_text: that, looking up, I saw a great ram standing opposite the gate. It had horns, one higher than the other, and the higher one was rising.

target_units.text: The ram you saw with the horns is the king of the Medes and Persians.

relationship: same-chapter reversal of the ram's invulnerability
rationale: At first no animal stands before the ram and no one rescues from its hands. When the goat strikes, the ram cannot stand and no one rescues it from the goat. The repeated inability to stand or rescue marks the reversal of power.
source_text: After this I saw the ram charging eastward, northward, westward, and southward. No animals stood before it, and no one rescued from its hands. It did as it wished and was exalted.

target_units.text: I saw it approach the ram, become furious with it, strike it, and shatter its two horns. The ram no longer had strength to stand against the goat. It hurled the ram down upon the earth and crushed it, and no one could rescue the ram from the goat.

relationship: same-chapter interpretation of the goat and its single horn
rationale: The goat arriving from the west has one horn between its eyes. The explanation calls the goat the king of the Greeks and the horn the first king. No name is supplied for that first king.
source_text: I was pondering, and a male goat came from the west over the earth’s surface without touching the earth. The goat had a single horn between its eyes.

target_units.text: The male goat is the king of the Greeks, and the great horn between its eyes is the first king himself.

relationship: same-chapter identification of the powers represented in the combat
rationale: The goat shatters and crushes the ram; the explanation identifies the ram with the Medo-Persian king and the goat with the Greek king. The interpretation provides the combatants' stated royal designations without adding a historical battle or date.
source_text: I saw it approach the ram, become furious with it, strike it, and shatter its two horns. The ram no longer had strength to stand against the goat. It hurled the ram down upon the earth and crushed it, and no one could rescue the ram from the goat.

target_units.text: The ram you saw with the horns is the king of the Medes and Persians.
The male goat is the king of the Greeks, and the great horn between its eyes is the first king himself.

relationship: close imagery of shattered rule divided toward the four winds
rationale: The goat's great horn is shattered and four horns arise toward heaven's four winds. The later account describes a kingdom shattered and divided toward those four winds, not according to the former ruler's might. The shared pattern is compared without naming the ruler.
source_text: The male goat grew exceedingly strong. When it became strong, its great horn was shattered, and four other horns rose behind it toward the four winds of heaven.

target_units.text: When he arises, his kingdom will be shattered and divided toward the four winds of heaven, not according to his might or the lordship with which he ruled. His kingdom will be removed, and he will teach others these things.

relationship: related emergence of an additional horn from an existing configuration
rationale: A strong horn sprouts from one of the four horns; the earlier vision has a small horn sprouting among ten. Both make an emerging horn prominent, but their starting configurations and descriptions differ.
source_text: From one of them a single strong horn sprouted. It grew strong and struck toward the south, toward the east, and toward the north.

target_units.text: and many plans were in its horns. Another single horn sprouted among them, small among its horns, and three of the earlier horns were withered through it. This horn had eyes like human eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and it made war against the holy ones.

relationship: related exaltation toward heaven's stars followed by downfall
rationale: The horn reaches the stars but is dashed to earth and trampled by them. Isaiah's lament against Babylon's king describes aspiration above the stars and descent to Hades. Daniel's stars act against the horn; they are not its trampled victims.
source_text: It was raised as high as heaven’s stars, but was dashed to the earth from the stars and trampled by them,

target_units.text: How the dawn-bearer who rises in the morning fell from heaven! The one dispatching to all the nations was shattered to earth.
You said in your mind, ‘I will ascend to heaven, set my throne above heaven’s stars, and sit on a high mountain, upon the high mountains toward the north.
I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’
But now you will descend to Hades and to the earth’s foundations.

relationship: related removal of sacrifice and devastation of the sanctuary
rationale: The source speaks of removed sacrifice and a sanctuary to be made desolate. The later passage describes defiling the sanctuary, removing sacrifice and establishing an abomination. This limited correspondence does not replace the source's ancient mountains with a different object.
source_text: until the chief commander rescues the captivity. Because of him the ancient mountains were dashed down; their place and sacrifice were removed. He set it down upon the earth, and it prospered and came to pass, and the sanctuary will be made desolate.

target_units.text: Arms from him will arise, defile the sanctuary of fear, remove the sacrifice, and establish an abomination of desolation.

relationship: related moral disorder alongside the prospering of wrongdoing
rationale: Daniel's vision places righteousness thrown to the ground beside action that prospers. Jeremiah asks why the impious person's way prospers. The connection concerns the troubling prosperity, without identifying the source's unspecified agent with an individual in Jeremiah.
source_text: Sins came upon the sacrifice; righteousness was thrown down to the ground, and he acted and prospered.

target_units.text: Thou art righteous, Lord, as I make my defense before Thee; nevertheless I will speak judgments with Thee. Why does the impious person’s way prosper? Why did all who commit acts of rejection flourish?

relationship: related questions about the completion of a vision and cleansing
rationale: A holy one asks how long the removed sacrifice and desolated holy places will remain. Daniel later asks the linen-clothed figure when the wonders will reach completion and be cleansed. The speakers differ, and their questions are not assigned an identical numerical answer.
source_text: I heard another holy one speaking, and the other said to the speaking Phelmouni, “How long will the vision stand, and the sacrifice that was removed, and the sin of desolation that was given, and the holy places be made desolate for trampling?”

target_units.text: I said to the one clothed in fine linen above, “When, then, will the wonders you have told me reach completion, and these things be cleansed?”

relationship: related cleansing of holy places after desecration
rationale: Daniel announces the sanctuary's cleansing after the stated evening-and-morning period. Judas and his brothers resolve to cleanse desolated holy places, and the priests carry out the cleansing. This is a thematic historical counterpart, not a calculation equating the dates or proving the stated period's fulfillment.
source_text: He said to him, “Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days; then the sanctuary will be cleansed.”

target_units.text: Judas and his brothers said, “Behold! Our enemies have been crushed. Let us go up to cleanse the holy places and dedicate them anew.”
The whole army gathered, and they went up to Mount Zion.
They saw the sanctuary desolate, the altar profaned, the gates burned down, plants growing in the courts as in a thicket or on one of the mountains, and the chambers demolished.
They tore their garments, lamented with a great lament, and put ashes on themselves.
They fell face down upon the ground, sounded the signal trumpets, and cried to Heaven.
Then Judas ordered men to fight those in the citadel until he had cleansed the holy places.
He chose blameless priests devoted to the law.
They cleansed the holy places and carried the stones of defilement to an unclean place.

relationship: parallel seeking of understanding within visions
rationale: Daniel seeks to understand while a human-like figure stands opposite him. In the earlier vision he approaches one standing there to seek exact understanding. The recurring interpretive setting is shared without asserting the figures' identity.
source_text: As I, Daniel, watched the vision, I sought to understand, and there stood opposite me someone with a human appearance.

target_units.text: and approached one of those standing there, seeking exact understanding from him concerning all these things. He answered me and explained the judgment of the words:

relationship: related appearance of Gabriel as a commissioned messenger
rationale: The voice calls on Gabriel to give Daniel understanding. In Luke, Gabriel says he stands before God and was sent to speak to Zechariah. Both name Gabriel's commissioned communication; the messages and recipients differ.
source_text: I heard a human voice in the midst of Ulai, calling, “Gabriel, give that one understanding of the vision.” The man cried out and said, “The vision concerns that command.”

target_units.text: The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel, who stands before God, and I was sent to speak to you and announce this good news to you.

relationship: parallel falling face down at a visionary encounter
rationale: Daniel is disturbed and falls on his face as the figure approaches and addresses him. Ezekiel likewise falls on his face upon seeing the appearance of the Lord's glory and hears a speaking voice. Daniel's appointed-hour statement is additional.
source_text: He came and stood beside where I stood. As he came, I was disturbed and fell upon my face. He said to me, “Understand, son of man, for this vision is still for an appointed hour.”

target_units.text: Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

relationship: parallel raising of a prostrate recipient to hear speech
rationale: Daniel, asleep face down, is touched and raised. Ezekiel is commanded to stand and is raised by a spirit to hear the speech. The comparable restoration of posture preserves the different means described.
source_text: As he spoke with me, I fell asleep face down on the ground. He touched me and raised me on the spot,

target_units.text: He said to me, “Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak to you.”
A spirit came upon me, took me up, raised me, and set me on my feet; I heard Him speaking to me,

relationship: related visions awaiting an appointed time of completion
rationale: Daniel is told that the reported events remain until the appointed time of completion. Habakkuk likewise describes a vision still for a season and rising toward the end. The particular events and the target's changing pronouns are not collapsed into one prediction.
source_text: and said to me, “Behold! I am reporting what will happen at the end of the wrath to the sons of your people; it will still remain until the hours of the appointed time of completion.

target_units.text: For the vision is still for a season, and it will rise toward the end and not toward emptiness. If he delays, wait for him, for coming he will come and certainly will not linger.

relationship: same-chapter explanation of the ram's royal significance
rationale: The interpretation identifies the ram as king of the Medes and Persians, pointing back to the great horned ram opposite the gate. It does not identify the higher and lower horns with named individual kings.
source_text: The ram you saw with the horns is the king of the Medes and Persians.

target_units.text: that, looking up, I saw a great ram standing opposite the gate. It had horns, one higher than the other, and the higher one was rising.

relationship: same-chapter explanation of the goat's royal significance
rationale: The Greek king and first king explain the goat and its single horn between the eyes. The link preserves the source's own interpretation without importing a name from later historical reconstruction.
source_text: The male goat is the king of the Greeks, and the great horn between its eyes is the first king himself.

target_units.text: I was pondering, and a male goat came from the west over the earth’s surface without touching the earth. The goat had a single horn between its eyes.

relationship: related division of royal power among successors
rationale: Daniel describes four kings from his nation arising, but not according to his strength. Maccabees describes Alexander dividing his kingdom among officers who take power and wear diadems. The target does not number them as four, and the comparison does not identify each horn or equate the succession details.
source_text: As for the four horns that were shattered and rose behind it, four kings of his nation will arise, but not according to his strength.

target_units.text: He summoned his distinguished officers, who had been brought up with him from his youth, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive.
Alexander reigned twelve years, and he died.
His officers took power, each in his own place.
They all put on diadems after his death, and their sons after them for many years; they multiplied evils on the earth.

relationship: related hostile powers characterized by shameless faces
rationale: The vision announces a king with a shameless face when sins reach fullness. The covenant warning describes a nation shameless of countenance that does not respect the old or pity the young. The facial characterization accompanies hostile power in both, while understanding riddles belongs only to Daniel's king.
source_text: At the end of their kingship, when their sins reach fullness, a king with a shameless face who understands riddles will arise.

target_units.text: The Lord shall bring against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, as the swooping of an eagle, a nation whose speech you shall not understand,
a nation shameless of countenance, which shall not regard the face of the aged, nor have mercy upon the young.

relationship: related hostile power prevailing against holy people
rationale: The ruler destroys rulers and a people of holy ones; the earlier horn wages war on holy ones and routes them. Both describe holy people suffering under a hostile power, without assigning the visions a proved common historical identity.
source_text: His strength will be made firm, though not by his own strength. He will destroy astonishingly, prosper, and act; he will destroy rulers and a people of holy ones.

target_units.text: I observed that horn waging war against the holy ones and routing them,

relationship: related destructive power operating through deception
rationale: Daniel describes prosperous falsehood, an exalted heart and many disappearing through deceit. The letter describes the lawless one's coming with false wonders and deceptive unrighteousness among those perishing. This compares destructive deception without resolving Daniel's gathering-of-a-hand phrase or identifying the actors.
source_text: His intent will be against the holy ones; falsehood will prosper in his hands, and his heart will be exalted. By deceit he will make many disappear, rise for the destruction of men, make a “gathering of a hand,” and sell.

target_units.text: His coming is according to the working of Satan, with all power and signs and wonders of falsehood,
and with every deception of unrighteousness for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved.

relationship: related closure of revelation until a future completion
rationale: The evening-and-morning vision is true but closed because many days remain. Daniel is later told to cover the commands and seal the book until completion. The latter passage's madness and injustice are preserved rather than replaced with increased knowledge.
source_text: The evening-and-morning vision was found to be true. Now the vision is closed up, for it is still for many days.”

target_units.text: But you, Daniel, cover the commands and seal the book until the time of completion, until the many go mad and the earth is filled with injustice.”

relationship: related bodily and emotional impact of visions on Daniel
rationale: Daniel is weak for many days, returns to royal affairs, and says he is undone by the vision. His earlier vision ends with astonishment and a changed condition. The shared impact does not make their durations or administrative aftermath identical.
source_text: I, Daniel, was weak for many days. Then I rose and again conducted royal affairs. I was undone by the vision, and there was no one who understood.

target_units.text: Until the account ended, I, Daniel, was greatly overcome with astonishment; my condition changed, and I fixed the matter in my heart.”

relationship: explicit connection to Jeremiah's seventy-year restoration word
rationale: Daniel considers the seventy years associated with Jeremiah and Jerusalem's reproach. Jeremiah's letter promises visitation and return when Babylon's seventy years are about to be fulfilled. The reference uses this edition's chapter 36, not a conventional alternative chapter number.
source_text: in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, considered in the books the number of years, when a command came to the land concerning Jeremiah the prophet, to bring Jerusalem’s reproach to its full term: seventy years.

target_units.text: Because thus said the Lord: When seventy years are about to be fulfilled for Babylon, I will visit you and establish My words for you, to return your people to this place.

relationship: parallel explicit association of Jeremiah, desolation and seventy years
rationale: Chronicles explains the captivity and the land's desolation in relation to Jeremiah's word and seventy years. Daniel likewise considers Jeremiah's seventy years concerning Jerusalem. Chronicles also supplies the transition to Cyrus without resolving Daniel's later week calculations.
source_text: in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, considered in the books the number of years, when a command came to the land concerning Jeremiah the prophet, to bring Jerusalem’s reproach to its full term: seventy years.

target_units.text: He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,
to fulfill the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth, until the land accepted its Sabbaths, to keep Sabbath. All the days of its desolation it kept Sabbath, to complete seventy years.

In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, after the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth had been fulfilled, the Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians. He ordered a proclamation throughout his kingdom in writing, saying,

relationship: parallel fasting and prayer in response to Jerusalem's distress
rationale: Daniel turns to prayer and mercy with fasting, sackcloth and ashes after considering Jerusalem's reproach. The report of Jerusalem's ruined walls leads to mourning, fasting and prayer in Nehemiah. Sackcloth and ashes are stated in Daniel, not added to the target.
source_text: I set my face toward the Lord God to find prayer and mercy, with fasts, sackcloth, and ashes.

target_units.text: They said to me, “The remaining people who were left from the captivity there in the country are in great distress and disgrace. Jerusalem’s walls have been pulled down, and its gates have been set ablaze with fire.”
When I heard these words, I sat down and wept, and mourned for days. I was fasting and praying before the God of heaven,

relationship: close confession of the great fearsome covenant-keeping God
rationale: Both prayers address the great and fearsome God who keeps covenant and mercy for those loving Him and keeping His commandments. The shared invocation precedes confession of the community's sins.
source_text: I prayed to the Lord God and confessed, saying, “Behold, Lord, Thou art the great, strong, and fearsome God, keeping the covenant and mercy for those who love Thee and guard Thy commands:

target_units.text: and said, “No, I pray, Lord, God of heaven, the Mighty One, the Great and Fearsome, who dost keep the covenant and mercy for those who love Him and keep His commandments:

relationship: close communal confession of sin, lawlessness and wrongdoing
rationale: Daniel confesses sin, wrongdoing, impiety and transgression. Solomon's prayer anticipates deportees returning and pleading that they have sinned, acted lawlessly and done wrong. The prayer describes the kind of confession Daniel makes without identifying a single formula word for word.
source_text: we have sinned, done wrong, acted impiously, fallen away, and transgressed Thy commandments and judgments,

target_units.text: and they turn their hearts in the land where they were deported, return, and plead with Thee in the land of their exile, saying, ‘We have sinned, acted lawlessly, and done wrong,’

relationship: parallel failure to heed God's prophetic messengers
rationale: Daniel admits that the people and their leaders did not listen to God's prophets. Chronicles describes God's repeated sending of prophets and the people's sneering and rejection before judgment. Daniel's enumeration of recipients is broader than the target's wording.
source_text: and have not listened to Thy servants the prophets, to what they spoke in Thy name to our kings, our rulers, our fathers, and every nation upon the earth.

target_units.text: The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent through prophets, rising early and sending His messengers, because He spared His people and His sanctuary.
They kept sneering at His messengers, treating His words as nothing, and mocking His prophets, until the Lord’s anger rose among His people, until there was no healing.

relationship: close penitential shame associated with sin and captivity
rationale: Daniel assigns righteousness to God and shame of face to scattered Israel. Ezra's prayer likewise confesses shame before God and describes captivity and shame of face because of lawless deeds. The shared language concerns acknowledged guilt rather than an assertion that the prayers were spoken together.
source_text: Righteousness belongs to Thee, Lord, but shame of face to us as on this day—to the people of Judah, those dwelling in Jerusalem, and all the people Israel, near and far, in all the countries where Thou didst scatter them because of the trespass they committed before Thee.

target_units.text: and said, “Lord, I am ashamed and abashed to lift my face toward Thee, for our lawless deeds have multiplied above our heads and our offenses have grown to heaven.

From the days of our fathers until this day we have been in great offense. In our lawless deeds, we, our kings and our sons have been handed over into the hand of the kings of the nations—to the sword, captivity, plunder and shame of our face—as on this day.

relationship: parallel inclusion of kings, rulers and fathers in national guilt
rationale: Daniel includes kings, rulers and fathers in the shame caused by sin. The communal prayer in Nehemiah names those groups in hardship and says they did not carry out God's law. Both refuse to exempt the nation's leaders and ancestors from confession.
source_text: Master, shame of face belongs to us, to our kings, rulers, and fathers, because we have sinned against Thee.

target_units.text: “Now, our God, the mighty, great, strong and fearsome One, who dost keep Thy covenant and Thy mercy, do not let all the hardship that has found us seem small before Thee—the hardship of our kings, rulers, priests, prophets, fathers and all Thy people, from the days of the kings of Assour until this day.
“Thou art righteous in all that has come upon us, for Thou hast acted in truth, while we have sinned grievously.
“Our kings, rulers, priests and fathers did not carry out Thy law or attend to Thy commandments and Thy testimonies by which Thou didst testify to them.

relationship: related divine mercy toward a sinful Israel
rationale: Daniel turns from acknowledged rebellion to the righteousness and mercy belonging to the Lord. The psalm says mercy and abundant redemption are with the Lord and promises Israel's redemption from lawless deeds. The target expressly states redemption, while Daniel here names God's mercy.
source_text: To the Lord belong righteousness and mercy, for we have fallen away from Thee

target_units.text: For with the Lord is mercy, and with Him is abundant redemption,
And He will redeem Israel from all its lawless deeds.

relationship: close confession of abandoning commands delivered through prophets
rationale: Daniel confesses failure to follow God's law set before Moses and the people through prophetic servants. Ezra's prayer confesses abandonment of commandments given through God's servants the prophets. Both connect disobedience with the mediated commands.
source_text: and have not listened to the voice of the Lord our God, to follow Thy law that Thou didst set before Moses and us through Thy servants the prophets.

target_units.text: What can we say, our God, after this? For we have abandoned Thy commandments,

which Thou gavest us through Thy servants the prophets, saying, ‘The land you are entering to inherit is a land being moved amid the movement of the peoples of the nations, in their repulsive practices, with which they have filled it from mouth to mouth in their uncleanness.

relationship: close fulfillment of written covenant curses after abandonment
rationale: Daniel identifies the curse and oath in Moses' law as having come upon sinful Israel. Deuteronomy explains devastation and removal to another land by abandonment of the covenant and the written curses. The connection grounds Daniel's appeal in the stated covenant sanctions.
source_text: All Israel abandoned Thy law and fell away, refusing to hear Thy voice. The curse and oath written in the law of Moses, God’s servant, came upon us, because we sinned against Him.

target_units.text: And they shall say, Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord, the God of their fathers, which He made with their fathers when He brought them forth out of the land of Egypt;
and they went and served other gods, and bowed down unto them, whom they did not know, and whom He had not allotted unto them.
And the Lord was kindled in wrath against that land, to bring upon it all the curses which are written in this book of the law.
And the Lord removed them from their land in wrath, and anger, and exceeding great indignation, and cast them into another land, as it is now.

relationship: related unparalleled suffering of Jerusalem under divine anger
rationale: Daniel describes Jerusalem's calamities as unequaled under heaven. The lament asks passersby whether there is pain like the city's pain on the day of the Lord's anger. Both stress the exceptional affliction without making their comparisons identical in form.
source_text: He established for us His commands, all He spoke against us and against our judges, all Thou didst judge for us, bringing great calamities upon us, such as had not occurred under heaven as occurred in Jerusalem.

target_units.text: Not to you, all who pass along the road! Turn and see whether there is pain like my pain, which came to be. Speaking against me, the Lord humbled me on the day of His furious anger.

relationship: parallel persistence in wrongdoing despite remembered calamities
rationale: Daniel confesses that the calamities did not lead to seeking God by abandoning sin. Addressing survivors in Egypt after describing Jerusalem's ruin, Jeremiah asks whether earlier evils were forgotten and says they still have not stopped or held fast to God's ordinances.
source_text: According to what is written in Moses’ covenant, all the calamities came upon us. Yet we did not seek the face of the Lord our God by departing from our sins and understanding Thy righteousness, Lord.

target_units.text: Have you forgotten your fathers’ evils, the evils of Judah’s kings, your rulers’ evils, and your wives’ evils, which they committed in Judah’s land and outside Jerusalem?
They have not stopped to this day and have not held fast to My ordinances, which I set before their fathers.

relationship: close acknowledgment of God's righteousness amid deserved calamity
rationale: Daniel affirms God's righteousness in all He does while confessing disobedience. Nehemiah's communal prayer likewise says God is righteous in all that came upon the people, while they sinned grievously. Both place the fault in the people's conduct.
source_text: The Lord God kept watch over the calamities and brought them upon us, for the Lord our God is righteous in everything He may do, and we did not listen to His voice.

target_units.text: “Thou art righteous in all that has come upon us, for Thou hast acted in truth, while we have sinned grievously.

relationship: related watchfulness to perform announced judgment
rationale: Daniel says God kept watch over the calamities and brought them. Jeremiah hears that God is watchful over His words to perform them, followed by the announcement of northern calamities and judgment on Jerusalem. The target's immediate object of watchfulness is His words.
source_text: The Lord God kept watch over the calamities and brought them upon us, for the Lord our God is righteous in everything He may do, and we did not listen to His voice.

target_units.text: The Lord said to me, You have seen well, because I am watchful over My words to perform them.
The Lord’s word came to me a second time, saying, What do you see? I said, A cauldron heated from beneath, its face away from the north.
The Lord said to me, From the north calamities will be kindled upon all who inhabit the land.

Because behold, I am summoning all the kingdoms from the north of the land, says the Lord. They will come and each set his throne at the forecourts of Jerusalem’s gates, against all her surrounding walls and against all Judah’s cities.
I will speak to them with judgment concerning all their evil, because they abandoned Me, sacrificed to foreign gods and bowed down to the works of their hands.

relationship: close recollection of deliverance from Egypt with an uplifted arm
rationale: Daniel recalls God bringing His people out of Egypt with an uplifted arm. Exodus records the promise to ransom Israel with an uplifted arm and bring them out of Egyptian oppression. The prayer recalls the saving action announced in the earlier promise.
source_text: Now, Master, Lord our God, who didst bring Thy people out of Egypt with Thine uplifted arm and didst make Thyself a name as on this day: we have sinned and acted in ignorance.

target_units.text: Go, say to the sons of Israel: ‘I am the Lord. I will bring you out from the Egyptians’ domination and deliver you from slavery. I will ransom you with an uplifted arm and with great judgment.
And I will take you to Myself for a people, and I will be your God; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the oppression of the Egyptians.

relationship: parallel plea against wrath and reproach after Jerusalem's devastation
rationale: Daniel asks wrath to turn from Jerusalem and calls the city and people a reproach among their neighbors. The psalm laments neighboring reproach, asks how long anger will last and petitions rescue and propitiation. Both connect the ruined community's shame with appeal for mercy.
source_text: Master, according to Thy righteousness, let Thy wrath and anger turn away from Thy city Jerusalem, Thy holy mountain. Because of our sins and our fathers’ acts of ignorance, Jerusalem and Thy people, Lord, are a reproach among all around us.

target_units.text: We became a reproach to our neighbors, sneering and ridicule to those around us.
How long, Lord? Wilt Thou be angry to the end? Will Thy jealousy blaze like fire?
Pour out Thy wrath upon nations that do not know Thee, and upon kingdoms that did not call on Thy name,
for they devoured Jacob and made his place desolate.
Do not remember our ancient acts of lawlessness; let Thy compassions swiftly reach us first, for we became very poor.
Help us, God our Savior. For the glory of Thy name, Lord, rescue us, and be propitious toward our sins for Thy name’s sake,

relationship: related appeal to God's face for restoration
rationale: Daniel asks God's face to look upon the desolate holy mountain. The psalm asks God to turn His people back and make His face shine so they will be saved. The source says look upon, while the target explicitly says shine.
source_text: Now, Master, hear Thy servant’s prayer and my supplications. Let Thy face look upon Thy desolate holy mountain, for Thy servants’ sake, Master.

target_units.text: God, turn us back; make Thy face shine, and we shall be saved.
Lord, God of powers, how long art Thou angry at the prayer of Thy servant,
wilt Thou feed us bread of tears and give us tears to drink by measure?
Thou madest us an object of contradiction for our neighbors, and our enemies sneered at us.
Lord, God of powers, turn us back; make Thy face shine, and we shall be saved. Diapsalma.

relationship: close contrast between reliance on mercy and human righteous deeds
rationale: Daniel grounds the supplication in God's mercy rather than the petitioners' righteous deeds. Titus describes salvation according to mercy rather than works done in righteousness. The shared basis is mercy; Daniel's prayer for the desolated city and the letter's washing and renewal remain distinct contexts.
source_text: Attend with Thine ear, Lord, and hear me. Open Thine eyes and see our desolation and that of Thy city, over which Thy name has been called. For we make our supplication in our prayers before Thee because of Thy mercy, not our righteous deeds.

target_units.text: But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for humanity appeared,
He saved us, not on the basis of works done by us in righteousness, but according to His mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit,
whom He poured out richly upon us through Jesus Christ our Savior,
so that, justified by His grace, we might become heirs in accordance with the hope of eternal life.

relationship: close appeal for forgiveness and rescue for God's name's sake
rationale: Daniel asks God to hear, act and be propitious for His own sake because His name is called over the city and people. The psalm petitions rescue and propitiation toward sins for the glory of God's name. Both make God's name a reason for the appeal.
source_text: Lord, be propitious! Lord, hear and act, and do not delay, for Thine own sake, Master, because Thy name has been called over Thy city Zion and Thy people Israel.”

target_units.text: Help us, God our Savior. For the glory of Thy name, Lord, rescue us, and be propitious toward our sins for Thy name’s sake,

relationship: parallel confession of personal and communal sins while praying
rationale: Daniel is confessing his own sins and Israel's sins in prayer. The prayer in Nehemiah likewise confesses Israel's sins and expressly includes the speaker and his father's house. Neither prayer places guilt only on other people.
source_text: While I was speaking in prayer, confessing my sins and the sins of my people Israel, and making supplication in prayers before the Lord my God and on behalf of our God’s holy mountain,

target_units.text: let Thine ear be attentive and Thine eyes opened to hear Thy servant’s prayer, which I pray before Thee today, day and night, for the sons of Israel, Thy servants. I confess concerning the sins of the sons of Israel that we have sinned against Thee. I and my father’s house have sinned.

relationship: parallel visit by Gabriel in a setting of prayer and worship
rationale: Gabriel reaches Daniel while he is praying at the hour of the evening sacrifice. In Luke, the people pray at the incense hour and Gabriel appears to the officiating priest. The settings involve prayer and liturgical time, but Luke's incense hour is not identified as Daniel's evening sacrifice.
source_text: while I was still speaking in my prayer, the man I had seen at first in my sleep, Gabriel, was carried swiftly and approached me at the hour of the evening sacrifice.

target_units.text: The whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.
An angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right of the altar of incense.
Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
But the angel said to him, “Do not fear, Zechariah, for your petition has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall name him John.
You will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth,
for he will be great before the Lord. He will certainly drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.
He will turn many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God.

He himself will go before Him in Elijah’s spirit and power, to turn fathers’ hearts toward children and the disobedient to the understanding of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a people made ready.”
Zechariah said to the angel, “How will I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.”
The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel, who stands before God, and I was sent to speak to you and announce this good news to you.

relationship: explicit return of Gabriel's role in giving understanding
rationale: Gabriel says he has come to show Daniel understanding. In the earlier vision the voice specifically commands Gabriel to give Daniel understanding. This connects the named messenger's repeated explanatory role.
source_text: He approached and spoke with me, saying, “Daniel, I have just come out to show you understanding.

target_units.text: I heard a human voice in the midst of Ulai, calling, “Gabriel, give that one understanding of the vision.” The man cried out and said, “The vision concerns that command.”

relationship: related response before prayer is completed
rationale: Gabriel says the command went out at the beginning of Daniel's supplication. Isaiah promises that God will listen before the people cry and respond while they are still speaking. Both describe prompt divine response, without equating the distinct settings or messages.
source_text: At the beginning of your supplication, a command went out from the Lord, and I came to explain it to you, because you are worthy of pity. Understand the command.

target_units.text: Before they cry out I will listen to them; while they are still speaking I will say, ‘What is it?’

relationship: related wiping away of injustice in a word of restoration
rationale: Daniel's announced purposes include injustices being wiped away and everlasting righteousness given. Isaiah identifies God as the One wiping out lawless acts and calls for their acknowledgment toward justification. The comparison concerns removal of sin, not an imported calculation of the seventy weeks or anointing of the holy of holies.
source_text: Seventy weeks have been determined for your people and the city Zion: for sin to be brought to completion, injustices to become scarce, injustices to be wiped away, the vision to be understood, everlasting righteousness to be given, the vision to be fulfilled, and a holy of holies to be gladdened.

target_units.text: I am, I am the One who wipes out your lawless acts, and I will certainly not remember.
But you, remember, and let us be judged. You, state your lawless acts first, so that you may be justified.

relationship: parallel announcement of Jerusalem's rebuilding
rationale: Daniel's command speaks of building Jerusalem as a city for the Lord. Isaiah announces that Jerusalem will be inhabited and rebuilt and the holy house founded. The link preserves the source's supplied wording and does not insert the conventional seven-week and sixty-two-week wording into this unit.
source_text: You will know, understand, and rejoice. You will find commands to be answered, and you will build Jerusalem as a city for the Lord.

target_units.text: and establish His servant’s words and make His messengers’ counsel true? He says to Jerusalem, ‘You will be inhabited,’ and to Judea’s cities, ‘You will be rebuilt,’ and her deserted places will spring up;
He says to the abyss, ‘You will be desolate, and I will dry your rivers’;
He tells Cyrus to understand, and says, ‘He will do all My wishes.’ He says to Jerusalem, ‘You will be rebuilt, and I will lay the foundation of My holy house.’”

relationship: related destruction of Jerusalem and its sanctuary by a foreign power
rationale: Daniel announces destruction of the city and sanctuary by a kingdom of nations. Jeremiah records Nebuzaradan burning the Lord's house and the city's houses, and the Chaldean force with him demolishing the wall. This is a bounded comparison of devastation, not an identification of Daniel's anointed one or a chronology equating the events.
source_text: After seven and seventy and sixty-two, an anointing will be removed and no longer exist. A kingdom of nations will destroy the city and sanctuary together with the anointed one. Its completion will come with wrath and last until the time of completion; it will be assailed by war.

target_units.text: In the fifth month, on the tenth of the month, Nebuzaradan, the chief guard who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned the Lord’s house, the king’s house, and all the city’s houses; every great house he burned with fire.
The Chaldean force with the chief guard pulled down the whole wall of Jerusalem all around.

relationship: explicit Gospel appeal to Daniel's abomination-of-desolation wording
rationale: Matthew names Daniel when speaking of the abomination of desolation standing in a holy place. Daniel here places an abomination of desolations upon the temple. The connection concerns the cited image; it does not normalize the source's distinctive numbers or derive a modern timetable.
source_text: The covenant will prevail for many. It will return again and be rebuilt in breadth and length. At the completion of times, after seven and seventy periods and sixty-two years, until the time of the completion of war, desolation will be removed when the covenant grows strong for many weeks. At the end of the week the sacrifice and libation will be removed. Upon the temple will be an abomination of desolations until completion, and completion will be given upon the desolation.”

target_units.text: So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of through Daniel the prophet standing in a holy place—let the reader understand—
then let those in Judea flee to the mountains.

relationship: related historical use of the abomination-of-desolation expression
rationale: Daniel describes an abomination upon the temple. Maccabees calls the installation upon the altar an abomination of desolation and gives a dated account. The shared expression is explicit, while an exact fulfillment of Daniel's numerical periods is not claimed.
source_text: The covenant will prevail for many. It will return again and be rebuilt in breadth and length. At the completion of times, after seven and seventy periods and sixty-two years, until the time of the completion of war, desolation will be removed when the covenant grows strong for many weeks. At the end of the week the sacrifice and libation will be removed. Upon the temple will be an abomination of desolations until completion, and completion will be given upon the desolation.”

target_units.text: On the fifteenth day of Chislev, in the one hundred and forty-fifth year, he built an abomination of desolation upon the altar. They built pagan altars in the surrounding cities of Judah.

relationship: shared first-year setting under Cyrus king of the Persians
rationale: Daniel's vision is dated to Cyrus's first year, and Chronicles dates the stirring of Cyrus and his proclamation to that first year. The particular reign-year setting is shared; the proclamation and Daniel's command are not asserted to be the same document.
source_text: In the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, a command was shown to Daniel, whose name was called Baltasar. The vision and command were true, and the strong multitude will understand the command; I understood it in a vision.

target_units.text: In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, after the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth had been fulfilled, the Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians. He ordered a proclamation throughout his kingdom in writing, saying,

relationship: related mourning accompanied by abstinence
rationale: Daniel's three-week mourning introduces the dietary abstinence described next. Ezra records Esdras mourning covenant-breaking and taking neither bread nor water. The connection concerns mourning with abstinence; Daniel's duration and the different stated diets are not harmonized.
source_text: In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks.

target_units.text: Esdras arose from before the house of God and went to the treasury chamber of Ioanan son of Elisoub. He went there, but ate no bread and drank no water, for he was mourning over the deported community’s covenant-breaking.

relationship: related episodes of Daniel abstaining from rich food and wine
rationale: Daniel abstains from desirable bread, meat and wine during mourning. Earlier he requests avoidance of the royal dinner and wine to avoid pollution, receiving legumes and water. The recurring restraint is shared, but its reason and duration differ and no complete fast is inferred from chapter 10.
source_text: I ate no desirable bread; meat and wine did not enter my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil until I completed the three weeks of days.

target_units.text: Daniel considered in his heart how he might avoid being polluted by the king’s dinner and the wine he drank, and petitioned the chief eunuch that he might not be contaminated.
The Lord gave Daniel honor and favor before the chief eunuch.

The chief eunuch said to Daniel, “I am anxious about my lord the king, who prescribed your food and drink, lest he see your faces drawn and weak beside the foreign youths being reared with you, and I risk my own neck.”
Daniel said to Abiesdri, appointed chief eunuch over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,
“Test your servants for ten days, and let us be given legumes from the earth to eat, and water to drink.
If our appearance looks drawn beside the other young men eating the royal dinner, then deal with your servants however you wish.”
He dealt with them in this manner and tested them for ten days.
After ten days their appearance was good and their bodily condition better than the other young men eating the royal dinner.
Abiesdri kept removing their dinner and wine and giving them legumes in exchange.

relationship: related linen-clothed figure in the river vision sequence
rationale: Daniel sees a man clothed and wrapped in fine linen beside the Tigris. The later river scene addresses the one clothed in fine linen above. The repeated clothing and river setting connect the descriptions without supplying an unspoken personal identity.
source_text: and I lifted my eyes and saw a man clothed in fine linen, with fine linen wrapped around his waist, and light coming from his middle.

target_units.text: I, Daniel, saw two others standing, one on this side of the river and one on the other.
I said to the one clothed in fine linen above, “When, then, will the wonders you have told me reach completion, and these things be cleansed?”

relationship: related visionary descriptions of flashing bronze, torches and lightning
rationale: Daniel's figure has flashing-bronze limbs, torch-like eyes and a lightning-like face. Ezekiel's creatures have feet sparkling like bronze, with fire like torches and lightning among them. The sensory imagery is shared; the figures and placement of each feature differ.
source_text: His body was like a tarshish stone, his face like a flash of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and feet like flashing bronze, and the sound of his speech like the sound of an uproar.

target_units.text: Their legs were straight, and their feet were winged, with sparks like flashing bronze; and their wings were light.
A human hand was beneath their wings on their four sides; and the faces of all four of them
did not turn as they walked; each went straight ahead.
The likeness of their faces was a human face and a lion’s face on the right for all four, and a calf’s face on the left for all four, and an eagle’s face for all four.
The wings of all four were stretched out above; each had two joined to one another, and two covered the top of their bodies.
Each went straight ahead. Wherever the spirit was going, they went and did not turn.
And amid the living creatures was an appearance like burning coals of fire, like the sight of torches whirling among the living creatures, and brightness of the fire; lightning came out of the fire.

relationship: parallel differing perceptions of recipients and their companions
rationale: Daniel sees the vision while his companions do not, becoming frightened and fleeing. The heavenly light flashes around Saul and he hears Jesus, while his companions hear the voice but see no one. The selective perception is comparable, but Acts says the companions stand speechless rather than flee.
source_text: I, Daniel, saw this great vision, but the men with me did not see it. Strong fear fell upon them, and they fled in haste.

target_units.text: As he traveled and drew near Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
He said, “Who art Thou, Lord?” He answered, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do.”
The men traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.

relationship: related loss of strength following Daniel's visions
rationale: Daniel is alone and without strength after seeing the great vision. The earlier vision leaves him weak for many days and undone. The source's spirit turning upon him for destruction is preserved rather than substituted with a conventional change-of-complexion reading.
source_text: I was left alone and saw this great vision. No strength remained in me; a spirit turned upon me for destruction, and I had no strength.

target_units.text: I, Daniel, was weak for many days. Then I rose and again conducted royal affairs. I was undone by the vision, and there was no one who understood.

relationship: related prostration during visionary speech with differing hearing language
rationale: Daniel says he did not hear the sound of the speech and had fallen face down. Earlier, as the figure spoke, he fell asleep face down and was raised by a touch. The shared posture is clear; hearing and sleep details are not flattened into the same wording.
source_text: I did not hear the sound of his speech; I had fallen face down upon the earth.

target_units.text: As he spoke with me, I fell asleep face down on the ground. He touched me and raised me on the spot,

relationship: parallel raising of a prostrate prophetic recipient
rationale: A hand raises Daniel onto his knees and the soles of his feet. Ezekiel is raised and set on his feet by a spirit. The acts restore posture for the encounter, while Daniel's knees and the different agents remain explicit.
source_text: He brought a hand toward me and raised me upon my knees, upon the soles of my feet.

target_units.text: A spirit came upon me, took me up, raised me, and set me on my feet; I heard Him speaking to me,

relationship: parallel command to stand and receive speech
rationale: Daniel is addressed and told to understand the commands and stand in his place. Ezekiel is told to stand on his feet so that he may be spoken to. Daniel's designation worthy of pity is not replaced by a different familiar epithet.
source_text: He said to me, “Daniel, you are a man worthy of pity. Understand the commands I speak to you, and stand in your place, for I have just been sent to you.” As he spoke this command with me, I stood trembling.

target_units.text: He said to me, “Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak to you.”

relationship: close reassurance not to fear because the recipient has been heard
rationale: Daniel is reassured that his word was heard from the first day of humbling himself. Gabriel tells Zechariah not to fear because his petition was heard. The announced outcomes differ, but both reassurances couple Do not fear with being heard.
source_text: He said to me, “Do not fear, Daniel. From the first day you set your face to understand and humble yourself before the Lord your God, your word was heard, and I entered because of your word.

target_units.text: But the angel said to him, “Do not fear, Zechariah, for your petition has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall name him John.

relationship: related portrayal of Michael in conflict
rationale: Michael comes to assist against the Persian king's general. Jude depicts Michael the archangel contending with the devil about Moses' body. Both portray Michael in conflict, without identifying the source's general as the devil or resolving that general's nature.
source_text: The general of the king of the Persians stood against me for twenty-one days. Then Michael, one of the foremost rulers, came to help me, and I left him there with the general of the king of the Persians.”

target_units.text: But Michael the archangel, when he was contending with the devil and disputing about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him, but said, “May the Lord rebuke you.”

relationship: related revelation of what will happen in the latter days
rationale: The messenger comes to show what will meet Daniel's people in the latter days. Earlier Daniel says God disclosed to Nebuchadnezzar what must happen in the last days. The explanatory purpose is shared while the immediate recipients and stated subjects differ.
source_text: He said to me, “I came to show you what will meet your people in the latter days, for the vision is still for days to come.”

target_units.text: but there is a God in heaven who uncovers mysteries, who has disclosed to King Nebuchadnezzar what must happen in the last days. O king, live for ever! This is the dream and the vision of your head upon your bed:

relationship: related silence and restored speech in prophetic encounters
rationale: Daniel turns his face to the ground and falls silent before the mouth-touch of the next unit. Ezekiel hears that his tongue will be bound and his mouth opened when God speaks. The source does not say God binds Daniel's tongue as He does in the target.
source_text: As he spoke these commands with me, I set my face toward the earth and fell silent.

target_units.text: I will bind your tongue, and you will become mute; you will not be a man rebuking them, for it is an embittering house.
But when I speak to you, I will open your mouth, and you will say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord: Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who disobeys disobey,’ for it is an embittering house.”

relationship: close hand touching the mouth in a prophetic encounter
